title: The Farm
strapline: Mucking out, milking and counting sheep — a whole working world in miniature.
intent: Anchor animal knowledge that children partly own already: names, young ('cow and calf, sheep and lamb'), sounds and what each animal gives us.
Connect food to its source — milk, eggs, wool and wheat start here, not at the supermarket.
Practise gentle, responsible care: animals in this world need feeding, mucking out and putting to bed, every single day.
Sort, group and count naturally — animals belong in fields and pens, and a missing sheep matters.
Grow sustained pretend narratives around real jobs: the vet's visit, lambing time, the tractor stuck in the mud.
implementation: Model the specific names — ewe, lamb, foal, calf, piglet — and the correct verbs: we milk the cow, shear the sheep, collect the eggs.
Set up real routines within the play: morning feed, mucking out, shutting the henhouse at 'night' — farms run on jobs, and children love jobs.
Sing the repertoire at the farm itself — Old MacDonald with the actual animals in hand turns a song into a matching game.
Wonder about food journeys while children play: 'this cow's milk — how does it get to our snack table?'
Add real materials — hay, straw, corn, wool fleece — so the sensory world matches the story.
Introduce a problem to solve: the gate's been left open, a lamb is poorly, the fox has been spotted — then step back.
Follow up with the real thing where you can: hatching eggs, a farm visit, growing wheat in a pot.
key_questions: What jobs does the farmer have to do before breakfast?
Where should the animals sleep tonight — and who goes together?
The gate was left open and a sheep is missing — how will we know which one?
What does this cow give us, and what do we give her back?
What do you think the vet will say about the poorly lamb?

impact.text: Children name the animals and their young — cow and calf, sheep and lamb, pig and piglet — and use farm-specific words like ewe, shear and harvest.
Children ask for and join in farm songs with the animals in hand, matching each verse to its figure.
Children handle the animals gently — carrying them carefully, settling them into the barn — and remind others that animals must be looked after.
Children sort the animals into fields and pens by kind, arguing sensibly about where the goats belong.
Children ask and answer real questions about where food comes from — whose milk, whose eggs, what the wheat turns into.
Children feed, muck out and tend the animals in role, replaying the farmer's routine from morning feed to shutting the henhouse.
Children narrate unfolding farm dramas — the tractor stuck in mud, lambing in the night, the vet's visit — directing the story as they go.
Children count animals in and out of fields and notice immediately when one sheep is missing from the flock.

enhancements: Real hay, straw and dried corn in shallow trays as bedding and feed for the pens.
Raw wool fleece to feel, pull and match to the sheep — with a picture strip from fleece to jumper.
A small-world mud patch (cocoa-powder dough or wet compost) for the tractor to get properly stuck in.
A vet's kit basket — bandages, a clipboard, an appointment book — parked beside the farm.
Egg boxes and pretend eggs for collecting, counting and 'selling' at a farm-gate stall.
A milk-to-butter provocation at group time: shake cream in a jar until it turns, then taste it on bread.
Planted wheat or grass seed in trays that becomes the farm's real, growing field.

playing_exploring: Real hay, fleece and corn pull children in through their hands before the story starts.
Children play out roles they know from books and visits — farmer, vet, tractor driver — and try them on for size.
active_learning: The farm's routine gives children jobs to see through: every animal fed, every gate shut, every egg collected.
Finding the missing sheep means checking every field — and children keep going until the flock is complete.
creating_thinking: Children link what they know — this animal, this food, this job — into their own explanation of how a farm works.
A problem dropped into the play (open gate, poorly lamb) sparks plans, predictions and negotiated rescues.
